primary_topics: Resource lecture at the Philippine Judicial Academy (PhilJA), February 16, 2007 -- invited by Chancellor Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera; topic: Democracy and Development: the Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance
Safeguarding liberty: courts as great equalizers; strict scrutiny; three landmark Panganiban Court decisions (Senate v. Ermita, Bayan v. Ermita, David v. Arroyo) as the governing examples
Nurturing prosperity: courts must defer to political branches; deferential interpretation; Tanada v. Angara (WTO) and La Bugal-B'Laan (Mining Law) as the governing cases
Rule of law: the distinction between libertarianism and authoritarianism; the constitutional duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion; martial law's failure as the governing historical proof
sub_topics: Topic as restatement: 'this topic is close to my heart. I believe it is a restatement of my own judicial philosophy of Liberty and Prosperity Under the Rule of Law'

Strict scrutiny: 'in litigations involving civil liberties, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the people, particularly the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed, and the weak. Laws and actions that restrict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity.'

Three landmark decisions of the Panganiban Court: (1) Senate v. Ermita -- upholding the right of Congress to summon executive officials for investigations in aid of legislation; (2) Bayan v. Ermita -- scuttling the Calibrated Preemptive Response (CPR) policy and ruling in favor of the people's right to peaceful assembly; (3) David v. Arroyo -- recognizing the fundamental rights of the people under a state of national emergency

Nurturing prosperity: 'I maintain that the judiciary has a duty to nurture prosperity and to alleviate poverty'; the 1987 Constitution commands the State to promote a just and dynamic social order; deferential interpretation of laws and executive actions in economic matters
Tanada v. Angara and La Bugal: the two governing cases for deferential interpretation

Rule of law as the differentiating standard: 'what differentiates libertarianism from authoritarianism is the rule of law. No person, no matter how powerful or talented, can be above the law. Everyone, rich or poor, powerful or powerless, must follow pre-agreed rules.'
Martial law as negative proof: 'during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress'

21st century judge's constitutional duty: 'the 1987 Constitution has imposed upon the entire judiciary the duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion committed by any branch or instrumentality of the government. By prudently exercising this constitutional duty, the 21st century judges are really pursuing their proper roles in the governance of our country.'

stances.claim: The three Panganiban Court decisions (Senate v. Ermita, Bayan v. Ermita, David v. Arroyo) are the definitive legacy of CJP's liberty-safeguarding mandate: Congress checked executive privilege; the CPR was struck down; fundamental rights were protected even in a state of national emergency. These three constitute the most complete expression of strict scrutiny for civil liberties in post-martial-law jurisprudence.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-decisions-as-liberty-legacy: the landmark cases as the empirical proof that the strict scrutiny standard was actually applied during CJP's term
stances.confidence: asserted as a judicial legacy evaluation

stances.claim: The 21st century judge's constitutional duty under Section 1 Article VIII -- to strike down grave abuse of discretion by any branch or instrumentality of government -- means that judicial governance is not an activist expansion but a constitutional mandate. Judges who exercise this duty are not being activist; they are being faithful to the Constitution.
stances.rhetorical_move: grave-abuse-duty-as-constitutional-mandate: the political question doctrine's Philippine limitation as the governing justification for judicial intervention in governance
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing constitutional interpretation

notable_anecdotes: Three landmark Panganiban Court decisions: (1) Senate v. Ermita -- congressional investigative power vs. executive privilege; (2) Bayan v. Ermita -- CPR policy struck down; the right to peaceful assembly maximum-tolerance standard restored; (3) David v. Arroyo -- fundamental rights protected under a state of national emergency. These three form the definitive liberty-safeguarding legacy of the Panganiban Court.

Martial law as the negative historical proof: 'during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress' -- the most direct historical argument against authoritarianism in the corpus.

21st century judge as governance actor: 'by prudently exercising this constitutional duty [to strike down grave abuse of discretion], the 21st century judges are really pursuing their proper roles in the governance of our country' -- the constitutional justification for judicial involvement in governance.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered February 16, 2007 as a resource lecture at the PhilJA -- invited by Chancellor Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera; topic: Democracy and Development: the Role of the 21st Century Judge in Governance -- CJP opens: 'this topic is close to my heart. I believe it is a restatement of my own judicial philosophy of Liberty and Prosperity Under the Rule of Law.' The lecture systematically applies the philosophy. On safeguarding liberty: strict scrutiny -- 'in litigations involving civil liberties, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the people, particularly the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed, and the weak. Laws and actions that restrict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity.' Three Panganiban Court landmark decisions: Senate v. Ermita (right of Congress to summon executive officials for investigations); Bayan v. Ermita (CPR policy scuttled; right to peaceful assembly upheld); David v. Arroyo (fundamental rights protected under a state of national emergency). On nurturing prosperity: courts must defer to political branches (deferential interpretation); Tanada v. Angara (WTO Treaty upheld) and La Bugal-B'Laan (Mining Law upheld) as the governing cases. On rule of law: 'what differentiates libertarianism from authoritarianism is the rule of law. No person, no matter how powerful or talented, can be above the law.' Martial law as the historical negative proof: 'authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.' Conclusion: the 1987 Constitution imposes upon the entire judiciary the duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion by any branch or instrumentality of government. 'By prudently exercising this constitutional duty, the 21st century judges are really pursuing their proper roles in the governance of our country.'
